Rudragāyatrī
(‘Gāyatrīmantra of रुद्र)
------------------------------------------
The Gāyatrīmantra of the Ṛgveda (3.62.10)—which has been repeated in other वेदस् also—has become so famous and popular that similar mantras in the same गायत्री meter on other deities of the Hindu pantheon, have appeared in many later works.
In the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣad (1.22-33) several such Gāyatrīmantras have been given. One such is the रुद्र-gāyatri (1.23) It runs as follows:
tatpuruṣāya vidmahe, mahādevāya dhīmahi, tanno rudraḥ pracodayāt ॥
[‘May we know or realise the Supreme Person. For that, may we meditate upon महादेव and to that meditation may रुद्र impel us’.]
The मन्त्र previous to this (1.22) is also, sometimes, called by the same name since the second and the third lines of this are similar to the रुद्रगायत्री.
This मन्त्र also, like the other gāyatrīmantras, is used for meditation and जप.
The Prapañcasāratantra (27.41) attributed to Śaṅkarācārya (A.

-820) gives a dhyānaśloka (verse describing the form of the deity for meditation) beginning with the words ‘bibhrad-dorbhiḥ’ and ending with ‘kalottuṅgamauliḥ’ for this रुद्र-गायत्री. It describes रुद्र as holding an axe and a deer in two hands and the other two showing the abhaya and the varada mudrās (handposes expressing protection and granting boons). He is sitting on a lotus, wearing the tiger-skin. His body is well-decorated. He has five faces (each with three eyes) and is shining like a mountain of precious stones.

rudrākṣa
(‘Rudra’s eye’)
------------------------------------------
The रुद्राक्ष is the berry of the tree or the shrub Elaeocarpus ganitrus, used to prepare Śaiva rosaries.
When रुद्र (Śiva) performed austerities for a thousand years with open eyes the tears that rolled out of his eyes (= akṣi) fell on the earth and grew into fine trees producing these berries. Hence the name रुद्राक्ष (or rudrākṣi).
It is well-known that रुद्र/Śiva has three eyes. From the eye representing सूर्य or the sun, 12 varieties of rudrākṣas, dark-brown in colour, were produced. From the second eye representing चन्द्र or the मोओन्, 16 varieties of white rudrākṣas were created. From the third eye representing अग्नि or the fire, 10 varieties of dark rudrākṣas were evolved.
Thus 38 varieties of rudrākṣas are stated to be in existence.
As regards the wearing of the rudrākṣas (strung with a cotton or silk thread) on the body, different colours are recommended for different varṇas as follows:
white ones for ब्राह्मणस्;
red or brown ones for kṣattriyas;
yellow or mixed coloured ones for vaiśyas;
and, dark or black ones for the शूद्रस्.
A रुद्राक्ष bead may be of different sizes—big, medium or small.
Also, its mukhas or faces may vary from one to fourteen. wearing of the different varieties on the body is said to produce different results.
For instance, wearing a necklace of rudrākṣas with one mukha or six mukhas can free a person from the sin of ब्रह्महत्या (killing of a ब्राह्मण); of ten mukhas, can get rid of the trouble created by evil spirits; of twelve mukhas, can vouchsafe freedom from diseases and enemies and so on.
Performing जप (repetition of the divine name) with a rosary of rudrākṣas duly consecrated is considered extremely auspicious. However, one should not wear this on the body.
Rudrākṣas strung with cotton or silk thread can be worn on different parts of the body, like the two arms, wrists, on the tuft of hair, in the neck, in the ears and on the chest. The number of beads on each has also been specified.
See also RUDRĀKṢA-JĀBĀLA-UPANIṢAD.

Rudrākṣa Jābāla Upaniṣad
------------------------------------------
This is a minor Upaniṣad assigned to the Sāmaveda. There are 49 sections comprising anuṣṭubh verses as also passages in prose.
It is in the form of a long dialogue between Kālāgni-रुद्र and sages like Bhusuṇḍa, Sanatkumāra, जडभरत, दत्तात्रेय, कात्यायन, वसिष्ठ and others. The topics dealt with may be summarised briefly as follows: (the numbers in the brackets indicate the verses or sections.)
Origin of रुद्राक्ष trees and beads (1-5); results of wearing the beads or doing जप with them (6 and 7); varieties of the रुद्राक्ष beads (8-16); methods of wearing the beads on the various parts of the body along with the appropriate mantras (17-25); rudrākṣas with one to fourteen faces and the results of wearing them (26-42); things to be given up or avoided by one who wears the beads (43); eulogy of wearing रुद्राक्ष on various occasions (44,45); greatness of रुद्राक्ष (46-48); eulogy of studying this Upaniṣad (49).
The Upaniṣad makes a special mention that one who wears the rudrākṣas must avoid eating meat, onion and garlic; nor should he consume liquor.
Another point stressed is that even if one does not wear it always, he can wear it on special days like eclipses, during the ayanas or equinoxes and saṅkrāntis (passage of the sun into the next zodiacal sign), full-मोओन् and new-मोओन् days.
See also RUDRĀKṢA.

Rudrayāmala
------------------------------------------
The yāmalas are a group of tāntrik literature. (See TANTRAS.) They represent the secret dialogues between a deity and his spouse (yāmala = pair).
Out of the eight yāmalas, the Rudrayāmala is the third.
The printed texts contain 66 chapters and 6000 verses, mostly in the anuṣṭubh metre, though the references to this work in treatises like the Dhanadāpura-ścaraṇa-vidhi, put the number at 1,25,000 verses.
It praises the Atharvaveda profusely.
Apart from dealing with the mysterious कुण्डलिनी and the yogic practices connected with it, quite a few elements of the वामाचार schools like the पञ्चमकारस् also find a prominent place.
In this work the गुरु’s place is supreme.
See also BRAHMA-YĀMALA.

Rudrapraśna
------------------------------------------
The Rudrapraśna is the fifth praśna (section) of the fourth kāṇḍa (chapter) of the Taittirīya Saṁhitā or the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It is also known as the Rudra or the Rudrādhyāya or the Namaka. It has eleven anuvākas or long stanzas.
God रुद्र, as his very name indicates, is a terrible deity, armed with a bow, arrows and a sword. If he is pacified with appropriate prayers, he will shower his mercy on the supplicant and fulfil his desires. This is the gist of the first अनुवाक.
The next eight anuvākas (2 to 9) describe the various forms and aspects of रुद्र, along with an obeisance (namaḥ) attached to each of the names. (Hence the name Namaka.)
Some of these aspects are: Hiraṇya-bāhu (golden-armed); Babhluśa (seated on the bull नन्दि); Harikeśa (with dark hair); स्थपति (master); Niceru (one who moves constantly); अश्वपति (leader of मोन्क्स्); Gṛtsapati (leader of intelligent persons); Bhava (origin of all beings); रुद्र (remover of all miseries); Śarva (destroyer of sins); पशुपति (lord of beings bound in सṁसार), Sahasrākṣa (one with a thousand eyes); Mīḍhuṣṭama (giver of rains); Saṁvṛdhvan (glorious one); Agriya (primeval being); Āśu (all-pervading); Ślokya (established in Vedic mantras); Dhṛṣṇu (adept in protecting); Vāstavya (one who resides in wealth); सोम (one who is with his consort Umā); Tāmra (who is red like the rising sun); Hantṛ (destroyer of enemies); Tāra (one who helps the jīvas to transcend सṁसार); Śambhu, शङ्कर (producer of happiness); शिव (the auspicious one); Tīrthya (purifier); Kapardin (one with matted hair).
The tenth अनुवाक is a long prayer asking for the following boons: freedom from misery and fear for all the members of the family and the livestock; a life of happiness for all, both in this world and in the next; withdrawal of (his) fierce form and granting a vision of (his) benign form; urging one’s organ of speech to praise रुद्र.
The last—the eleventh—anuvāka describes the innumerable forms that रुद्र takes, and obeisance is offered.
Before starting a Vedic sacrifice, a वेदि or a platform of bricks had to be built. After keeping the last brick in place, it used to be bathed in milk—called ‘abhiṣeka’—with the mantras of this Rudrapraśna.
There is a time-honoured tradition that the Rudra or Namaka and Camaka (Taittirīya Saṁhitā 4.7) are to be chanted daily along with the Puruṣasūkta.
There are several methods of chanting the Rudrapraśna (and Camaka) ceremonially. One such method prescribed by the sage शातातप is as follows:
Rudra: Chant the Namaka (Rudra) once, followed by the first अनुवाक of Camaka. This is repeated a second time and so on, each time adding the next अनुवाक of the camaka, the total chanting being eleven times. This is called a ‘Rudra’.
Rudraikādaśinī: If eleven persons chant the रुद्र (as stated above) eleven times or one person recites it 121 times, it becomes ‘Rudraikādaśinī’.
Mahārudra: This is achieved if eleven persons recite the रुद्र eleven times a day for eleven days.
Alternatively, if 121 persons chant it eleven times or 1331 persons chant it once, in a day, it becomes ‘Mahārudra’.
Atirudra: If eleven persons chant it 11 times per day for 121 days, it becomes ‘Atirudra’.
The same will be the result if 1331 persons chant it eleven times in a day (just for one day), or, 114,641 persons recite it once, in a day.
Generally, महारुद्र and अतिरुद्र are performed to ward off calamities for the society or the country.
See also ATIRUDRA.

Rudra
(‘the terrible’)
------------------------------------------
Rudra is a Vedic deity. He has been eulogised in only three sūktas of the Ṛgveda out of which two are more explicit (1.11

). His name appears 75 times. He is also called ‘Śiva’ 18 times.
The various definitions of the word रुद्र are: one who roars or thunders; one who makes his enemies weep; one who destroys the सṁसार (transmigratory existence) of his devotees; one who destroys अज्ञान or nescience.
Rudra’s beauteous form has been described in various mantras. He is strong with powerful arms. He has a long जटा or hair. He is very handsome. His body decorated with many ornaments of gold, especially a matchless necklace, is brilliant. He is holding a वज्रायुध (thunderbolt) as also a strong bow and arrows.
When necessary he can also assume a fierce form. Riding in a chariot, he charges at our enemies if only we pray to him.
Rudra is also full of mercy and a great protector of his votaries.
Being closely associated with forests and mountains, he is also the king of medicines and hence a healer of all diseases.
When supplicated, he destroys sins and grants happiness.
The Rudrapraśna of the Taittirīya Saṁhitā (4.5) gives a long and beautiful description of रुद्र.
The Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad (3.2) describes him as the creator and ruler of the universe.
The Mahābhārata (Anuśāsanaparva ch. 14) as also quite a few पुराणस् declare रुद्र as that form of शिव who destroys the universe at the end of a cycle of च्रेअतिओन्.
In Vedic literature, sometimes eleven Rudras are mentioned. They may be minor deities representing the ten prāṇas (vital-airs) and the मिन्द् (See ŚIVA for details.)
In later literature (vide पद्म-purāṇa, Svargakhaṇḍa, ch. 8), eight names of रुद्र are mentioned, which are actually the eight aspects of रुद्र-शिव.
All the Rudras have their female counterparts or consorts like Rudrāṇī (Rudra), भवानी (Bhava), Śarvāṇī (Śarva), Śivānī (Śiva), Mahādevī (Mahādeva) and so on.
The eight Rudras or eleven Rudras, when considered as aspects of रुद्र-शिव, are described in detail, along with their garments and weapons, in iconographical works like Rūpamaṇḍana and Viśva-karmaśilpa.
Rudra is also regarded as having created bhūtas (demons), pretas (disembodied spirits), piśācakas (goblins) and kūṣmāṇḍas (malignant imps), who form his retinue.
See also ŚIVA.

Rudragītā
------------------------------------------
The Bhagavadgītā, the finest jewel among the secondary scriptures of Hinduism—generally called the smṛtis—has been responsible, though indirectly, for the appearance of several gītās in the later religious literature.
The Rudragītā is one of the minor gītās that occur in the Bhāgavata (4.24.33-79).
Prācīnabarhi was a great king. He had ten sons, all of whom were known as Pracetas. He commanded them to beget worthy sons after performing severe austerities. As they were proceeding, searching for a suitable place, they saw रुद्र, the great god, emerging out of a vast and beautiful lake.
The Pracetas then went towards him and offered their obeisance with great devotion. Pleased with this, god रुद्र taught them a wonderful hymn by which they were advised to pray to भगवान् वासुदेव.
It is this part comprising 47 ślokas or verses that has come to be known as the Rudragītā.
The following is a brief summary of the same:
Victory unto the Supreme Lord who protects the knowers of the आत्मन् (the Self). He is everything and everybody. He is the creator and controller of the world. He manifests himself through the four व्यूहस् or emanations. (See VYŪHAS.) It is he who is in the form of the deity सोम (the ड़ोओद् of gods), the lord of yajñas (sacrifices) as also the Virāṭpuruṣa (Cosmic Being). He, it is, who is कर्म (action) as well as its fruits. He is रुद्र as also ब्रह्मा. He is the origin of speech.
O Lord! Grant us the vision of your extremely elegant form.
(The next eight verses [45-52] give a highly poetical description of the well-known कृष्ण-वासुदेव form to facilitate meditation.)
One who wants to purify himself should meditate on this form.
He is easy of attainment for those who are deeply devoted to him.
One who has succeeded in pleasing him does not desire for anything else. None, including यम (the god of death), can exercise any control over such a devotee. The company of such devotees is far superior even to स्वर्ग (heaven) or मोक्ष (liberation).
Hence none should waste his time and life, but worship him, the origin of the world as also its destroyer as kāla or time.
Anyone who sings or chants this Rudragītā, especially in the early hours of morning, will be liberated from all bonds.

Rudraprayāga
------------------------------------------
There are plenty of places of पिल्ग्रिमगे in the lower and upper regions of the Himālayan ranges. रुद्रप्रयाग is one of them. It is in the Tehri-Garhwal district of Uttaranchal.
It is situated at the confluence of the rivers अलकनन्दा and Mandākinī, the tributaries of गङ्गा. It is in the middle of the route that leads to बदरीनाथ and केदारनाथ. In fact, it is from here that the two roads get separated.
There is a nice temple of Rudranātha-शिव here, at the place where the sage नारद is stated to have performed severe austerities to please him. शिव is said to have given him a thorough knowledge of the science and art of मुसिच्.
The place is 135 kms. (84 miles) from the well-known pilgrim centre Hṛṣīkeśa (Rishikesh).
